questions.q: What is "Linux" in the strictest sense?
questions.explain: The kernel is a single program that schedules processes, manages memory, talks to hardware and implements the filesystem abstraction. `uname -r` shows the kernel build.

questions.q: What does a distro (distribution) add around the kernel?
options: A package manager, init system, standard directories, default config and curated packages
questions.explain: Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch and Alpine ship the same kernel source but differ above it.

questions.q: How do ordinary programs like bash or ls touch hardware?
options: By asking the kernel through a system call, since they run in unprivileged user mode
questions.explain: Only the kernel runs in privileged mode.

questions.q: Why can some scripts that work elsewhere break on Alpine?
options: It swaps GNU coreutils and glibc for BusyBox and musl
questions.explain: That substitution changes behaviour of some tools and libraries.

questions.q: What is the order of boot stages?
options: Firmware, bootloader, kernel, initramfs, switch_root to systemd (PID 1)
questions.explain: Each stage fails in a recognizable way.

questions.q: What is initramfs?
options: A temporary root filesystem in RAM with just enough tools (udev, disk/RAID/LUKS drivers) to find and mount the real root
questions.explain: The real root may be on an encrypted LVM volume.

questions.q: What does UEFI read boot entries from?
options: An EFI System Partition (a small FAT32 partition)
The first sector of the disk only
questions.explain: Legacy BIOS scanned a disk's first sector.

questions.q: What does switch_root do?
options: Replaces the initramfs root with the real root filesystem and execs the init system as PID 1
questions.explain: On most modern distros that's systemd.

questions.q: Where is system-wide configuration usually found?
questions.explain: If you're hunting for where X is configured, start in /etc.

questions.q: What belongs in /var?
options: Data that changes while the system runs: logs, caches, spool files
questions.explain: For example /var/log and /var/cache.

questions.q: What are /proc and /sys?
options: Virtual filesystems, not files on disk
questions.explain: `stat -f /proc` reports Type: proc with zero blocks.

questions.q: Why is /root kept separate from /home?
options: So the superuser's home is never accidentally on a separate, possibly-unavailable mount
questions.explain: /home holds regular users' directories.

questions.q: What does an inode NOT store?
questions.explain: The name lives in a directory entry, a (filename, inode number) pair in the parent directory.

questions.q: After `ln original.txt hardlink.txt`, how do the two relate?
options: Two names for the same inode, and stat shows Links: 2
questions.explain: ls -i shows the same inode number, 135 in the lesson.

questions.q: What happens to a symlink if you delete its target?
options: It breaks: cat gives 'No such file or directory'
questions.explain: A symlink is a separate tiny file whose content is just a path.

questions.q: After rm original.txt, does cat hardlink.txt still work?
options: Yes, because the inode survives while another link exists
questions.explain: The data is freed when the link count reaches zero (and no process has it open).

questions.q: Does the kernel know usernames?
options: No: it checks numeric UIDs/GIDs, and /etc/passwd and /etc/group are just lookup tables for humans
questions.explain: If a user is deleted while their UID still owns files, ls -l shows the bare number.

questions.q: In which order does the kernel check permission classes, and what happens at the first match?
options: Owner, then group, then other; it stops at the first match
questions.explain: So an owner with a more restrictive owner row than 'other' still gets only the owner row.

questions.q: In the lesson, with mode 311 (-wx--x--x) on a directory, what works for its owner?
options: cat project/notes.txt works, but ls project is denied, because there's no read bit
questions.explain: Read on a directory allows listing names; execute allows traversing into it.

questions.q: What does execute (x) mean on a directory?
options: Permission to run it as a program
Permission to traverse it (access entries by name)
questions.explain: Listing requires read (r).

questions.q: Why can an unprivileged user run /usr/bin/passwd and update /etc/shadow?
options: It's owned by root with the SUID bit, so it runs with the owner's UID
questions.explain: The `s` in -rwsr-xr-x marks SUID.

questions.q: What does SGID on a directory do?
options: New files inside inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group
questions.explain: The standard way to make a shared team directory.

questions.q: What does the sticky bit (t) do on a directory like /tmp?
options: Only a file's owner can delete or rename it, regardless of write permission on the directory
questions.explain: /tmp is drwxrwxrwt.

questions.q: What is mode 2775 on team-shared (after chgrp testeng)?
options: rwxrwsr-x with SGID, so files created there get group testeng
questions.explain: The lesson's touch team-shared/report2.txt shows group testeng.

questions.q: What do fork() and exec() each do?
options: fork copies the calling process (new PID); exec replaces the program in the same PID
questions.explain: The shell uses fork then exec to start every command.

questions.q: What values does fork() return?
options: 0 to the child, and the child's PID to the parent
questions.explain: This tells the two processes apart.

questions.q: What is special about PID 1?
options: It's the one process the kernel starts directly during boot (systemd), with PPID 0, and everything else descends from it
questions.explain: Losing it is fatal.

questions.q: Why do kernel worker threads like kworker appear in brackets in ps?
options: They're created by the kernel (children of kthreadd, PID 2), not by fork/exec from userspace, and have no real command line
questions.explain: ps -ef --forest draws the tree by PPID.

questions.q: What are file descriptors 0, 1 and 2 by convention?
questions.explain: It's a convention the kernel doesn't enforce.

questions.q: What does `cmd > file 2>&1` do?
options: Points fd 1 at the file, then fd 2 at wherever fd 1 now points, so both go to the file
questions.explain: The lesson's first ls /nonexistent wrote the error into cmd.log.

questions.q: What does `cmd 2>&1 > file` do?
options: stderr goes to where stdout pointed (the terminal) first, then stdout goes to the file, so errors still print to the terminal
questions.explain: Order matters: the second run left cmd2.log empty.

questions.q: How can you inspect a process's open descriptors?
options: ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd, a directory of symlinks, one per descriptor
questions.explain: fd 0 pointed to /dev/null in the example.

questions.q: What is the difference between dpkg and APT?
options: dpkg installs .deb files and keeps the on-disk database but resolves nothing; APT fetches from repositories and resolves dependency graphs, then hands installation to dpkg
questions.explain: rpm and DNF split the same way for the Red Hat lineage.

questions.q: What does `dpkg -L curl` show?
options: The package's exact file manifest, which is what apt remove deletes and nothing more
questions.explain: dpkg -S /usr/bin/curl does the reverse: which package owns a file.

questions.q: What three things does 'install this package' really involve?
options: Unpack files, record which files belong to the package, and verify dependencies
questions.explain: The record is what makes clean uninstalls possible.

questions.q: What does `apt-cache depends curl` list?
options: Its dependencies, such as libcurl4t64, libc6 and zlib1g
questions.explain: APT resolves that whole graph.

questions.q: What does debootstrap do?
options: Downloads and unpacks just enough .deb packages into a target directory to make a minimal root filesystem, without booting anything
questions.explain: Debian and Ubuntu installers use it internally.

questions.q: Why does debootstrap have a second stage that runs inside chroot?
options: So package postinst scripts execute in the new filesystem's environment rather than against the host
questions.explain: The first stage unpacks core packages.

questions.q: What does --variant=minbase mean?
options: The smallest useful set of packages rather than a full default install
questions.explain: --arch lets you build for another architecture, such as arm64 for a Raspberry Pi.

questions.q: Why bind-mount /dev and mount proc and sysfs inside the chroot?
options: So tools inside see device nodes and the /proc and /sys virtual filesystems
questions.explain: The chroot reported Ubuntu 24.04 while the host was 26.04.

questions.q: What does state D mean, and can SIGKILL stop it?
options: Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on disk I/O; it can't be killed until the I/O completes
questions.explain: The kernel considers the operation too delicate to abort.

questions.q: What is a zombie (Z) process?
options: A process that has exited but whose parent hasn't collected its exit status; kill -9 can't remove it
questions.explain: It has no running code left to signal. The parent must wait() or die.

questions.q: What do kill -STOP and kill -CONT do?
options: Move a process between S (sleeping) and T (stopped), like Ctrl-Z and fg/bg
questions.explain: The lesson showed S → T → S with ps.

questions.q: What is a signal, per the lesson?
options: Not a forceful interrupt but a flag the kernel sets that the target process, if in a position to, gets a chance to act on
questions.explain: That's why kill -9 sometimes does nothing.

questions.q: What does a higher nice value mean?
options: More generous to others: a smaller claim on the CPU (range -20 to 19)
questions.explain: Default is 0; -20 is the most aggressive.

questions.q: In the lesson's ps output, how does PRI relate to NI?
options: Lower PRI tracks higher (less favourable) nice: nice 0 showed PRI 19, nice 10 showed 9, nice 15 showed 4
questions.explain: ni is what you set; pri is procps's view of the kernel-level priority.

questions.q: What does renice do?
options: Changes the niceness of an already running process, e.g. to deprioritise a batch job without restarting it
questions.explain: Raising priority (lower nice) requires root.

questions.q: What does `chrt -p $$` report for a normal shell?
questions.explain: SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR are real-time policies.

questions.q: Why does `free -h` show a tiny 'free' but a large 'available'?
options: Much of memory is used as reclaimable page cache (buff/cache), which the kernel can free when needed
questions.explain: In the lesson, 1.0 GiB was free but 3.3 GiB available, with 2.5 GiB in buff/cache.

questions.q: What does virtual memory give each process?
options: Its own private address space, mapped to physical pages by page tables (4 KiB pages on most systems)
questions.explain: It also enables fork's copy-on-write and swapping.

questions.q: How was the OOM kill in the lesson triggered?
options: systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=100M ran a script in a memory-limited cgroup, and the kernel killed it (CONSTRAINT_MEMCG)
questions.explain: dmesg showed 'Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process'.

questions.q: What does the VM in the lesson lack that is common on cloud VMs and containers?
questions.explain: free -h showed 3.8 GiB total and no swap.

questions.q: What are LVM's three layers?
options: Physical volumes (PVs) pooled into a volume group (VG), with logical volumes (LVs) carved out of the pool
questions.explain: An LV can span multiple physical disks.

questions.q: Why does LVM make growing storage easier than partitions?
options: Growing an LV is a software operation against the VG's free space, not a disk-geometry problem
questions.explain: Partition resizing means shuffling data to make room.

questions.q: How did the lesson simulate two physical disks?
options: Two 512 MB plain files attached as loop devices with losetup
questions.explain: The files became /dev/loop0 and /dev/loop1.

questions.q: What order of commands builds a usable LVM filesystem?
options: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, mkfs.ext4, then mount
questions.explain: Then df -h confirms the mounted size (770M of an 800M LV after overhead).

questions.q: What do the six fstab fields mean, in order?
options: Mount, device, label, UUID, type, flags
Device, mount point, type, options, dump flag, fsck pass number
Name, size, type, owner, group, mode
Path, inode, type, options, time, size
questions.explain: fsck pass 1 is for root, 2 for others, 0 for never.

questions.q: Why identify a device by LABEL in fstab rather than /dev/vda1?
questions.explain: A hardcoded path breaks if /dev/vda1 becomes /dev/vda2.

questions.q: What does a bind mount do?
options: Makes the same directory's contents visible at a second path; it's not a new filesystem
questions.explain: Writes through either path affect the same files; container runtimes use this to expose host directories.

questions.q: How does findmnt differ from fstab?
options: findmnt shows the live mounts, which can differ from fstab if something was mounted by hand
questions.explain: fstab is a declarative list for boot time.

questions.q: What is a target in systemd?
options: A special unit that groups other units as a synchronization point, like multi-user.target
questions.explain: Units declare WantedBy=multi-user.target to start as part of reaching it, which is how systemctl enable works.

questions.q: What does After= in a unit file mean?
options: An ordering constraint only, not a dependency; Wants=/Requires= express need
questions.explain: ssh.service is deliberately tolerant of a not-fully-ready network.

questions.q: What does ConditionPathExists=!/etc/ssh/sshd_not_to_be_run do?
options: A runtime gate: the unit is skipped if that file exists
questions.explain: The ! negates the condition.

questions.q: Which unit type starts its service lazily on first connection?
questions.explain: A .timer is the scheduled-trigger unit.

questions.q: What problem does OnUnitActiveSec= avoid compared with cron?
options: A job overlapping itself, because it runs N seconds after the previous run finished
questions.explain: A 5-minute job scheduled every 5 minutes can overlap if one run takes 6 minutes under cron.

questions.q: What does `Type=oneshot` on heartbeat.service mean?
options: It runs once at boot only
It runs a command to completion and then becomes inactive (dead) until triggered again
questions.explain: systemctl status showed inactive (dead) with status=0/SUCCESS between timer runs.

questions.q: What do you run to enable a timer and start it right now?
questions.explain: It creates the symlink under timers.target.wants.

questions.q: Where does the service's output go with a timer-based job?
options: Through the normal journald pipeline, with no mail or separate logging setup
questions.explain: systemctl status also shows when it last ran and whether it succeeded.

questions.q: How does a journal entry differ from a syslog text line?
options: It's a structured record with named fields, several attached automatically by the journal
questions.explain: Examples: _UID, _GID, _BOOT_ID, _SYSTEMD_CGROUP.

questions.q: Why can journalctl -u filter by unit even for programs that never use systemd APIs?
options: The filtering key comes from the environment the message was logged in (the cgroup/unit), not from parsing text
questions.explain: Programs writing to stdout or stderr under a unit still get unit, UID, GID, cgroup and boot ID fields.

questions.q: What do CODE_FILE, CODE_FUNC and CODE_LINE show?
options: The source location, present only when the program uses sd_journal_print()-style calls
questions.explain: Plain stdout logging doesn't include them.

questions.q: What does an existing /var/log/journal directory indicate?
options: Persistent journal storage (otherwise logs live in memory and are lost at reboot)
questions.explain: The lesson's `journalctl --disk-usage` showed 8M.

questions.q: What do the leading c and b in ls -l on a device file mean?
options: c is a character device (stream); b is a block device (fixed-size blocks)
c is copy; b is backup
c is config; b is binary
questions.explain: /dev/null is c; /dev/vda is b.

questions.q: What do the major and minor numbers identify?
options: Major: which driver handles the device; minor: which specific instance the driver should talk to
questions.explain: /dev/null (1,3) and /dev/zero (1,5) share major 1 and differ by minor.

questions.q: What does udev do?
options: Names newly detected devices and creates symlinks such as disk/by-path and disk/by-diskseq
questions.explain: udevadm info shows the S: symlink lines.

questions.q: Why is /dev/vda major 253 in the lesson's VM?
options: It's a virtio_blk paravirtualised disk; real hardware would show a different major for its driver
questions.explain: The major identifies the driver.

questions.q: What does `ps -eo ... --sort=-pcpu` reveal about two cpu_hog.sh loops?
options: They're in state R at about 100% CPU each, dwarfing every other process
questions.explain: R means runnable: on a CPU or waiting for one.

questions.q: Why did uptime's load average look low (0.00, 0.05, 0.04) right after starting the hogs?
options: Load average is an exponentially decaying moving average over 1/5/15 minutes, so it takes wall-clock time to rise
questions.explain: The samples were taken in the first couple of seconds.

questions.q: In the vmstat output, what did the two hogs show?
options: us (user CPU) about 50% and id about 50%, with r = 2 runnable processes
questions.explain: A 2-CPU VM with two spinning loops uses half the CPU in user mode on average.

questions.q: What does an infinite `while true; do :; done` loop simulate?
options: A process stuck in a bad loop or spinning instead of blocking on I/O: a realistic incident pattern
questions.explain: The kernel schedules it like any CPU-bound process.

questions.q: What is the loopback interface (lo) for?
options: Letting a machine talk to itself without touching real hardware
questions.explain: A real NIC, a virtual device or lo can each be an interface.

questions.q: What does `scope link` on an address mean, versus `scope global`?
options: link is valid only on the local network segment (like IPv6 link-local); global is routable beyond this machine
questions.explain: The lesson's fe80:: address has scope link.

questions.q: What does `dynamic` on an inet address indicate?
options: It came from DHCP, with valid_lft/preferred_lft lease timers, so it can change
questions.explain: Nothing on the system owns the IP permanently.

questions.q: What does `ip route get 8.8.8.8` show?
options: The kernel's actual routing decision: next hop (via 192.168.5.2), interface and source address
questions.explain: Anything outside the local /24 uses the default route via the gateway.

questions.q: What does the hosts: files dns line in nsswitch.conf mean?
questions.explain: That's why a /etc/hosts entry overrides DNS.

questions.q: Why does /etc/resolv.conf show nameserver 127.0.0.53?
options: It's systemd-resolved's local stub resolver; the real upstream server (192.168.5.2) is shown by resolvectl status
The network's DNS server is localhost
questions.explain: The file says 'Do not edit'.

questions.q: What does resolvectl query github.com show?
options: One real resolution end to end: the address, the link, time taken and the protocol used
questions.explain: In the lesson: 22.2 ms via DNS.

questions.q: Which layer is consulted first for any program calling getaddrinfo()?
questions.explain: resolv.conf comes into play only when resolution falls through to dns.

questions.q: What is Netfilter?
options: The kernel subsystem with hook points (prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting) that iptables and nftables configure
questions.explain: Neither iptables nor nftables is netfilter itself.

questions.q: What does `iptables -V` showing `(nf_tables)` mean?
options: The iptables command is a compatibility layer that translates rules into nftables
questions.explain: It doesn't touch the legacy ipt_* modules.

questions.q: What does this nft rule do? `nft add rule inet demo input ip saddr 10.99.99.99 drop`
options: Drops incoming packets from source 10.99.99.99 in a chain attached to the input hook
questions.explain: The chain was created with type filter hook input.

questions.q: Where did the LIMADNS chain in the VM's ruleset come from?
options: Lima's own networking setup, redirecting DNS traffic for the VM
questions.explain: nft list ruleset shows the system's actual configuration.

questions.q: What does a LISTEN socket represent?
options: A server announcing it will accept new connections on a port; the kernel queues handshaken connections until accept()
questions.explain: ESTABLISHED is an active two-way conversation.

questions.q: What uniquely identifies an ESTABLISHED connection?
options: The pairing of a local address:port with a remote address:port
questions.explain: The lesson showed both ends of 127.0.0.1:8899 and 127.0.0.1:38698.

questions.q: What does `ss -tlnp` list?
options: TCP listening sockets with numeric ports and the owning process
questions.explain: -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p process.

questions.q: What does listening on 0.0.0.0:22 versus 127.0.0.1:8899 mean?
options: 0.0.0.0 accepts on all interfaces; 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections
questions.explain: systemd-resolved listens on 127.0.0.53 and 127.0.0.54 on port 53.

questions.q: What is the difference between a host key and a user key?
options: A host key proves the server's identity to you; a user key proves your authorisation to the server
questions.explain: authorized_keys and ssh-copy-id are built around user keys.

questions.q: Why does SSH warn loudly 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED'?
options: A host key almost never changes, so a change could be re-provisioning or a man-in-the-middle, and SSH can't tell which
questions.explain: It catches both causes.

questions.q: Why must the host private key be mode rw-------?
options: sshd refuses to use a key file with overly permissive permissions, and a readable private key defeats its purpose
questions.explain: The public key is world-readable, as it should be.

questions.q: What does ssh-agent hold, and what does `ssh-add -l` list?
options: Loaded identities in memory; their fingerprints
questions.explain: It showed the demo-key's SHA256 fingerprint.

questions.q: What question does a Linux Security Module answer that rwx permissions don't?
options: Can this specific program, regardless of which user runs it, do this specific thing — even for root
Can this user read this file
questions.explain: It's mandatory access control layered on top of owner/group/other.

questions.q: How do AppArmor and SELinux differ?
options: AppArmor is path-based with per-executable profiles; SELinux is label-based with contexts (user:role:type:level)
questions.explain: AppArmor is Ubuntu/Debian's default; SELinux is Red Hat/Fedora's.

questions.q: In the lesson, why did sshd show 'unconfined' while dig showed 'dig (enforce)'?
options: A profile exists and is enforced for dig but not for sshd on that system; having some profiles doesn't confine every process
questions.explain: /proc/<pid>/attr/current reveals a process's confinement.

questions.q: What does aa-status report?
options: How many profiles are loaded and in enforce or complain mode
questions.explain: The lesson showed 180 loaded, 103 enforcing, 2 complain.

questions.q: What are the two mechanisms that make a container look isolated?
options: Namespaces (what a process can see) and cgroups (what it can use)
questions.explain: A container is a normal Linux process on the host kernel.

questions.q: In the unshare PID-namespace demo, what PID did bash report for itself?
options: 1, genuinely what getpid() returns inside the namespace
questions.explain: ps aux inside saw only three processes.

questions.q: Why was --mount-proc needed?
options: Otherwise /proc would still show the host's process table through the mount namespace
questions.explain: It mounts a fresh /proc for the new PID namespace.

questions.q: Which namespace isolates the hostname, which plain chroot does not?
questions.explain: Others: network, user (UID/GID mapping), IPC and cgroup.

questions.q: How does the sysctl name net.ipv4.ip_forward map to the filesystem?
questions.explain: Reading or writing the file has the identical immediate effect.

questions.q: What does net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 do?
options: Lets the kernel route packets between interfaces (an endpoint becomes a router)
questions.explain: sysctl -w takes effect immediately, no reboot.

questions.q: How do you make a sysctl setting persist across reboots?
options: Put it in a file under /etc/sysctl.d/
questions.explain: For example 99-lima.conf.

questions.q: What does net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0 do?
options: Lets unprivileged users bind ports below 1024
questions.explain: Ports under 1024 are traditionally root-only.

questions.q: What does `auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_watch` do?
options: Watches /etc/passwd for write and attribute-change access, tagging events with the key passwd_watch
questions.explain: touch caused one matching event.

questions.q: What does an audit record give you that an inotify-style 'file changed' event doesn't?
options: A forensic record: process, real vs audit UID, syscall and success or failure, tied to a rule key
questions.explain: It's suited to compliance reviews and incident investigation.

questions.q: What was the real tooling mismatch in the lab?
options: ausearch -k found nothing although grep found the event in the raw audit log
questions.explain: Probably a parsing mismatch between the ausearch version and the log format.

questions.q: What lesson does the mismatch teach?
options: Know the raw log location (/var/log/audit/audit.log) and sanity-check a 'no matches' result against it
questions.explain: Otherwise you might believe a real event never happened.

questions.q: What does the project combine to build a 'container' by hand?
options: unshare namespaces (PID, mount, UTS) and a cgroup v2 memory limit
questions.explain: No container runtime is involved.

questions.q: How is the shell placed into the limited cgroup?
options: By writing its PID to the cgroup's cgroup.procs; memory.max sets the ceiling
questions.explain: Everything it spawns afterwards is in the group too.

questions.q: What happened when python allocated memory past 50M?
options: The kernel OOM-killed it inside the cgroup (CONSTRAINT_MEMCG); the shell reported 'Killed'
questions.explain: dmesg showed 'Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process'.

questions.q: Why does hostname inside show minicontainer while the host still shows lima-linuxlab?
options: The UTS namespace isolates the hostname, unlike plain chroot
questions.explain: --uts adds it to the PID and mount namespaces.

questions.q: In top's %Cpu(s), what does wa mean?
options: Time spent waiting on I/O: CPU idle but not free, something is blocked on disk or network
questions.explain: us is user mode, sy is kernel, id is genuinely idle.

questions.q: Why is 'avail Mem' much larger than 'free' in top?
questions.explain: 3340.9 available versus 1018.4 free in the lesson.

questions.q: Why is iostat's %util misunderstood?
options: It measures time with outstanding I/O, not percent of disk capacity or throughput headroom; check await and aqu-sz too
questions.explain: Don't size storage decisions on it alone.

questions.q: What does the `1 zombie` in top's Tasks line refer to?
options: The leftover sshd zombie seen in the earlier process-states lesson
questions.explain: A zombie is an exited process whose parent hasn't collected it.

questions.q: What does strace show?
options: Every system call a running process makes
questions.explain: ltrace shows library calls; perf shows where CPU time goes.

questions.q: What did `strace -c ls /tmp` reveal?
options: Even a simple command made 159 syscalls and hit 12 errors
questions.explain: Locale lookups, mmap of libraries and terminal checks add up.

questions.q: What did strace show about cat's failed openat of a locale .ftl file?
options: ENOENT: a harmless lookup that cat silently tolerates before opening the real file
questions.explain: It answers 'why is this program touching that path' with evidence.

questions.q: What does strace -e trace=open,openat do?
options: Filters output to just those syscalls
questions.explain: It makes long traces readable.

questions.q: When is the `none` I/O scheduler often the right choice?
options: For fast NVMe storage, where the device's own queues do better than software reordering
questions.explain: Reordering has a cost, and skipping it is correct when the device doesn't need help.

questions.q: What does mq-deadline prioritise?
options: Fairness and bounded latency, so no request waits indefinitely
questions.explain: bfq optimises interactive responsiveness on slower devices.

questions.q: Why was `rotational = 1` on a virtio disk surprising?
options: It tells the kernel it's a spinning disk, but the 1.4 GB/s throughput shows it's flash-backed; virtualisation made the hint unreliable
questions.explain: The flag wasn't correctly propagated through the virtual device.

questions.q: What does nr_requests = 256 mean?
options: The queue depth the block layer holds before applying backpressure to the application
questions.explain: It's visible in /sys/block/vda/queue/.

questions.q: What does `insmod hello.ko` do, and how do you confirm it loaded?
options: Loads the module into the running kernel; lsmod | grep hello shows it
questions.explain: The usage count of 0 means nothing depends on it, so rmmod is safe.

questions.q: Where did the module's printk messages appear?
options: In the kernel log, via dmesg
questions.explain: One message on init, one on exit.

questions.q: Why does the build need /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/build?
options: It compiles against the running kernel's real headers and build system
It holds the source of the module
questions.explain: The Makefile calls make -C ... M=$(PWD) modules.

questions.q: What were the two build warnings about?
options: The compiler and pahole versions differ from those that built the shipped kernel, usually harmless for simple modules but risky for complex ones
questions.explain: pahole generates BTF debug metadata.

questions.q: What does `ls -l /proc/$PID/fd` reveal about a running process?
options: Exactly what it has open: files, sockets and pipes, without attaching a debugger
questions.explain: The example showed a listening socket (fd 3) and a file opened for writing (fd 4).

questions.q: What does /proc/$PID/wchan show?
options: The kernel function the process is currently blocked in (e.g. hrtimer_nanosleep)
questions.explain: It matched time.sleep(60) in the script.

questions.q: Why was reading /proc/$PID/syscall refused without sudo?
options: Yama's ptrace_scope only allows inspecting direct ancestors or descendants by default
questions.explain: sudo bypassed the restriction.

questions.q: What does /proc/$PID/syscall show?
options: The raw syscall number and argument registers the process is currently inside
questions.explain: Syscall 115 on that architecture is nanosleep-family.

questions.q: How can you validate a new fstab line before a reboot?
options: Run mount -a, which attempts every entry as boot would
questions.explain: It caught a missing mount point in the lesson.

questions.q: What happens at boot when a non-root fstab entry fails?
options: systemd can't reach the dependent target and drops to an emergency shell for a human to intervene
questions.explain: It doesn't silently continue in a broken state.

questions.q: What are two common fstab failure modes?
options: The device doesn't exist, or the mount point doesn't exist (mkdir -p may be all that's missing)
questions.explain: Both can be tested on a running system.

questions.q: What does journalctl --list-boots show?
options: The boots recorded in the journal; the VM had only one
questions.explain: It's the command to check earlier boots for a failure.

questions.q: What is a container, compared with a VM?
options: A normal process on the same running kernel with a restricted view of resources; a VM boots a separate kernel on virtualised hardware
questions.explain: There's exactly one kernel involved for a container.

questions.q: Why is creating a container so fast?
options: It's just a new process with extra kernel bookkeeping (namespaces, a cgroup); `unshare --pid --mount-proc --fork true` took about 13 ms
questions.explain: A VM's boot measures in seconds to minutes.

questions.q: How was the VM's boot time measured in the lesson?
options: systemd-analyze: kernel 317ms, initrd 1.3s, userspace about 2m45s (mostly cloud-init network wait)
questions.explain: A real kernel boot and full userspace startup are unavoidable costs.

questions.q: What's a mistake in choosing between them?
options: Choosing a VM 'to be safe' where properly configured container isolation would suffice
questions.explain: The right tool depends on the isolation needed.

questions.q: What differs between mainstream distros, and what doesn't?
options: Package manager, release model and defaults differ; kernel and systemd features like permissions, namespaces and netfilter are the same
questions.explain: The lesson is documentation-based because it can't be verified on one distro.

questions.q: How do Fedora and RHEL relate?
options: Fedora is the fast-moving upstream; RHEL (and Rocky, AlmaLinux) is the long-support downstream built from a Fedora base
questions.explain: It mirrors Ubuntu's LTS philosophy.

questions.q: What is Arch Linux's release model?
options: Rolling release: there is no 'Arch 26.04'; the system continuously updates (pacman)
questions.explain: The philosophy differs from Debian and RHEL.

questions.q: Which default LSM do Ubuntu/Debian and RHEL/Fedora use?
options: AppArmor for Debian/Ubuntu; SELinux for RHEL/Fedora
questions.explain: Both use systemd init.

questions.q: What are the three kernel.org lines?
options: Mainline (newest, least tested), stable (bugfix backports for a few months) and longterm (bugfixes for years)
questions.explain: Distros and embedded systems build on longterm lines.

questions.q: Is the newest longterm kernel the newest mainline release?
options: No: LTS is a deliberate choice for specific releases (6.18 longterm versus 7.3 mainline in the data)
questions.explain: A kernel needn't be the newest to be fully supported.

questions.q: How many longterm lines were receiving updates in the lesson's data?
questions.explain: It was fetched live from kernel.org/releases.json.

questions.q: Why does the lesson fetch live release data?
options: Version numbers go stale, so check current data rather than memory
questions.explain: The output will look different by the time you read it.

questions.q: What makes `appuser` a least-privilege setup?
options: A dedicated user with key-only SSH (authorized_keys 600, .ssh 700, no password) running the service
questions.explain: The service also runs as appuser under systemd.

questions.q: What does curl returning 000 mean when the service is stopped?
options: No HTTP status at all: nothing is accepting the connection, so check systemctl status (inactive (dead))
questions.explain: It points away from an HTTP-level problem.

questions.q: What does Fault 2 in the lesson illustrate?
options: A firewall rule silently dropping a port that is listening, which ss -tln shows as LISTEN while connections still fail
questions.explain: The listener exists, but the packets never reach it.

questions.q: Which pieces does the capstone combine?
options: Users and SSH keys, a systemd service, an nftables rule, and diagnosis with the course's tools
questions.explain: Three faults were injected on purpose and diagnosed.

questions.q: A directory has mode 311 (d-wx--x--x) and you are its owner. `ls project` fails with 'Permission denied' but `cat project/notes.txt` works. Why?
options: The owner can never list a directory
There is no read bit, so listing names is denied, but execute lets you traverse into it by name
questions.explain: Read on a directory lists names; execute allows access by name. Verified: chmod 311 gives d-wx--x--x.

questions.q: With umask 022, what modes do a new file and a new directory get? With umask 077?
questions.explain: New files start at 666 and directories at 777, minus the umask. Verified by creating them: 644/755 and 600/700.

questions.q: A shared project directory should make every new file belong to the team group automatically. Which setting?
options: SGID on the directory (chmod 2775, group set to the team): drwxrwsr-x
questions.explain: SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group. Verified: chmod 2775 shows drwxrwsr-x.

questions.q: Anyone may create files in /tmp but only a file's owner may delete it. Which bit, and how does it appear?
options: The sticky bit, shown as t: drwxrwxrwt (mode 1777)
questions.explain: Verified: chmod 1777 gives drwxrwxrwt.

questions.q: `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows -rwsr-xr-x root root. What does the s mean for a normal user running it?
options: The program runs with the file owner's (root's) UID, so it can update /etc/shadow
questions.explain: SUID applies for the lifetime of that process only.

questions.q: You run `ln original.txt hardlink.txt` and `ln -s original.txt symlink.txt`, then `rm original.txt`. What happens?
options: cat hardlink.txt still works (the inode survives with 1 link); the symlink is broken
questions.explain: A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symlink stores a path. Verified by running the commands: link count 2 → 1, hardlink prints hello, symlink broken.

questions.q: `ls /nonexistent 2>&1 > cmd.log` leaves cmd.log empty and prints the error to the screen. Why?
options: stderr was duplicated onto the terminal first; only afterwards was stdout redirected to the file
questions.explain: Redirections apply left to right. `> cmd.log 2>&1` captures both. Verified by running both orders.

questions.q: A process shows state Z in ps and `kill -9` does nothing. What is it, and what removes it?
options: An uninterruptible sleep; send SIGKILL again
A zombie: it already exited, so there's nothing to signal; the parent must collect its status (or die, so init reaps it)
questions.explain: A zombie is just an exit-status record.

questions.q: A process is stuck in state D (uninterruptible sleep) on disk I/O. Will SIGKILL end it immediately?
options: No: it can't be killed until the I/O completes
questions.explain: The kernel considers the operation too delicate to abort.

questions.q: `free -h` shows 1.0Gi free but 3.3Gi available. Is the system low on memory?
options: No: much of it is reclaimable page cache (buff/cache), which counts as available
questions.explain: Look at available, not free.

questions.q: A service must run 'every 5 minutes' without overlapping itself if a run takes 6 minutes. Which mechanism fits best?
options: A systemd timer using OnUnitActiveSec= (runs after the previous run finished)
questions.explain: OnUnitActiveSec counts from the end of the last run. Output also goes to journald.

questions.q: You added a new line to /etc/fstab. How do you check it without rebooting?
options: Run `sudo mount -a`, which attempts every entry as boot would
questions.explain: A bad non-root entry can drop the next boot into an emergency shell.

questions.q: `/etc/resolv.conf` says `nameserver 127.0.0.53`. Where do DNS queries really go?
options: To the internet's root servers directly
To systemd-resolved's local stub, which forwards them to the upstream server shown by `resolvectl status`
questions.explain: nsswitch.conf's hosts: files dns line decides that /etc/hosts is checked first.

questions.q: A service is listening on port 9090 (`ss -tln` shows it), but remote connections time out while local ones work. What is the most likely cause?
options: A firewall rule dropping the port (check nft list ruleset / iptables)
questions.explain: The capstone's Fault 2: the socket is LISTENing, yet packets never reach it.

questions.q: `curl` returns HTTP status 000 for your service. What does it tell you?
options: No HTTP exchange took place: nothing accepted the connection (service stopped, wrong port or firewall), so check the service and socket first
questions.explain: Status 000 means curl got no HTTP response.

questions.q: Which two kernel mechanisms make a process look like a container, and what does each do?
options: Namespaces limit what it can see (PID, mount, UTS, network, user…); cgroups limit what it can use (CPU, memory…)
questions.explain: A container is a normal process on the host kernel.

questions.q: A process in a cgroup with memory.max=50M tries to allocate more. What happens?
options: The kernel OOM-kills it inside the cgroup (CONSTRAINT_MEMCG); the host keeps running
questions.explain: dmesg shows 'Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process'.

questions.q: Why does `iptables -V` print (nf_tables) on modern distros?
options: iptables is the old kernel subsystem
iptables is a compatibility front end that translates rules into nftables, both configuring netfilter's hooks
questions.explain: Neither tool is netfilter itself.

challenges.title: Redirection order
challenges.prompt: Using the emit function (writes one line to stdout and one to stderr), write redirections so that: A) both streams end up in both.log, B) stdout goes to out.log and stderr to err.log, C) demonstrate the common mistake by writing `2>&1` BEFORE `> wrong.log`, capturing what leaks to the terminal with $( ). Print the results exactly as shown in the expected output.
challenges.starter:
emit() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }

# A: send both streams into both.log
emit # your redirection here
echo "A: $(wc -l < both.log | tr -d ' ') lines"

# B: stdout to out.log, stderr to err.log
emit # your redirection here
echo "B: out=[$(cat out.log)] err=[$(cat err.log)]"

# C: wrong order
leaked=$(emit) # your redirection here
echo "C: leaked=[$leaked] wrong.log=[$(cat wrong.log)]"
challenges.expected:
A: 2 lines
B: out=[to stdout] err=[to stderr]
C: leaked=[to stderr] wrong.log=[to stdout]
challenges.solution:
emit() { echo "to stdout"; echo "to stderr" >&2; }

# A: send both streams into both.log
emit > both.log 2>&1
echo "A: $(wc -l < both.log | tr -d ' ') lines"

# B: stdout to out.log, stderr to err.log
emit > out.log 2> err.log
echo "B: out=[$(cat out.log)] err=[$(cat err.log)]"

# C: wrong order - stderr is duplicated onto the terminal (here, captured by $( ))
leaked=$(emit 2>&1 > wrong.log)
echo "C: leaked=[$leaked] wrong.log=[$(cat wrong.log)]"
challenges.explain: `> file 2>&1` points fd 1 at the file and then fd 2 at wherever fd 1 now points. With `2>&1 > file`, fd 2 is duplicated onto the terminal first, so errors still leak. Verified by running the solution in bash: output matches.

challenges.title: Hard link versus symlink
challenges.prompt: Create original.txt containing hello, a hard link hardlink.txt and a symlink symlink.txt. Print the link count of original.txt, delete the original, then show whether the hard link and the symlink still work and the link count that remains.
challenges.starter:
echo hello > original.txt
# create a hard link and a symlink to original.txt

echo "links before: $(ls -l original.txt | awk '{print $2}')"
rm original.txt
echo "hardlink: $(cat hardlink.txt)"
if [ -e symlink.txt ]; then echo "symlink: works"; else echo "symlink: broken"; fi
echo "links after: $(ls -l hardlink.txt | awk '{print $2}')"
challenges.expected:
links before: 2
hardlink: hello
symlink: broken
links after: 1
challenges.solution:
echo hello > original.txt
ln original.txt hardlink.txt
ln -s original.txt symlink.txt
echo "links before: $(ls -l original.txt | awk '{print $2}')"
rm original.txt
echo "hardlink: $(cat hardlink.txt)"
if [ -e symlink.txt ]; then echo "symlink: works"; else echo "symlink: broken"; fi
echo "links after: $(ls -l hardlink.txt | awk '{print $2}')"
challenges.explain: A hard link is a second directory entry for the same inode (link count 2), so the data survives rm. A symlink is a separate tiny file holding a path, which breaks when the target disappears. Verified by running the solution in bash: output matches.
